column2: having touched or conversed (with them) he is purified by looking at the sun; likewise on seeing a menstruating woman, a renunciate, a fallen person, a corpse.
Those of unrighteous conduct, a woman after childbirth, a eunuch, a naked person, the lowest of outcastes, those who carry the dead, and those who delight in others' wives —
this very purification of oneself is to be done by the wise: one should avoid unfit food, beggars, hypocrites, cats, asses and cocks,
the fallen, the cast-out, Chandalas, and eaters of the dead; the knower of dharma is purified by bathing on touching a menstruating woman, a village boar,
and likewise persons defiled by birth-impurity. One in whose house daily loss of the daily rite occurs,
and the lowest of men, who is abandoned by Brahmins and eats sin, should never cause loss of the daily rite.
Its non-performance I shall tell, only in cases of death and birth: a Brahmin should remain ten days without gifts and oblations;
a Kshatriya twelve days, a Vaishya half a month, and a Shudra a month, abandoning their own work.
After that all should do their own work as is fitting. Water should be given to the dead, going outside, by the gotra-kin.
On the first, fourth, seventh and ninth days, and likewise the collecting of his bones should be done by the gotra-kin on the fourth day.
After the collecting of bones, touching of their limbs is ordained; and all rites should be done by gotra-kin after the collecting.
Touch alone for sapindas on the day of death and for both; in accordance with the meaning, by choice, for those bound by weapons, rope, fire,
dead by poison, heat and the like, by fasting to death, a child, one in another country, and a renunciant who has died —
immediate purity for men; three days of impurity is stated. If a sapinda of sapindas dies when another has died,
the former purification is declared, the daily rites are to be done there. This same rule is seen even in birth-impurity.
For sapindas among sapindas, as appropriate, and for those with water-giving, when a son is born the father's bath with clothes is ordained.
If there another person follows after that, purification there too is stated by the days of the earlier birth.
After ten, twelve, a month, or a half-month's days have passed, all varnas should do their own rites by rule.
Then Ekoddishta should be done for the dead, and gifts should be given to Brahmins by the wise.
Whatever is dearest in the world and whatever is dear to him in the house, that should be given to the virtuous by one wishing it to be imperishable.
When the days are complete, having touched water, vehicles and weapons, all varnas who have given pindas and water to the dead and done the rites
should all do them purely for welfare hereafter and here. The three Vedas should be studied constantly; the wise should be so.
Wealth should be gained by dharma and sacrifice carefully done, so that one's self, Brahmins, is not enraged or reproached.
That should be done without fear which is not to be hidden from the great. Thus acting, Brahmins, a man in the house, being good,
obtains dharma, wealth and desire, and auspiciousness hereafter. This secret is life-giving, blessed, increasing wisdom,
removing all sin, holy, granting fortune, nourishment and health, auspicious, giving fame and renown to men, increasing brilliance and strength.
It should always be practised by men, the best means of heaven, by Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas and Shudras, best of sages;
it should be known with great effort by those seeking welfare, rightly. One who, knowing it, always practises it at the right time
is freed from all sins and honoured in the heavenly world. This most essential of essences has been told, best of Brahmins:
the dharma declared in Shruti and Smriti should not be given to just anyone; not to a non-believer, nor to one of wicked mind, Brahmins; not to a hypocrite, a fool, or one who prattles bad arguments.
Friendship, absence of longing, and likewise absence of meanness, best of Brahmins, and freedom from envy are the common virtues told for the varnas.
These are the common marks of all the ashramas; virtues and subsidiary duties of Brahmins and the rest are these, Brahmins.
Kshatriya action is told for a Brahmin, and Vaishya action in distress; for a Kshatriya, Vaishya action; for these two, Shudra actions.
When one is capable, both are to be given up, Brahmins; that should be done only in distress; one should not mix actions.
Thus the duties of the varnas have been told by me today, Brahmins; as I now properly speak the dharma of the ashramas, listen.
A boy who has undergone initiation, intent on learning the Veda, living in his teacher's house, Brahmins, a celibate student, composed,
devoted to purity and conduct, should do service to his teacher there. Observing vows, the Veda is to be acquired by the one whose mind is resolved.
At both twilights, Brahmins, he should worship the Sun and likewise the fire, composed, and should salute his teacher.
When the teacher stands he should stand, when he goes he should follow, when he sits he should sit low; the pupil, best of Brahmins, should give up what is adverse.
He should recite the Veda as told by him, not with distracted mind, standing in front; and with the teacher's permission he should eat the alms-food.
He should enter the water after the teacher has entered; he should bring him firewood, water and the like, and be ready when needed.
Having acquired the Veda to be acquired, having obtained permission then, the wise one, having discharged his debt to the teacher, should enter the householder stage.
Having obtained a wife by rule, and wealth by his own work, the householder should do all the householder's duties, Brahmins, to the best of his ability:
worshipping ancestors with libations, gods with sacrifices, guests with food, sages with Vedic study, Prajapati with offspring,
beings with the offering, and the entire world with truthful speech; a man obtains worlds earned by his own actions.
Those who live on alms, wandering mendicants and celibates, also rest here on the householder state, which is therefore supreme.
For the business of acquiring the Veda, for bathing at holy places, and for seeing the earth, Brahmins roam the earth.
Those who are homeless and foodless and who stay at whatever house at evening have the householder as their constant support and origin.
They should be given welcome and gifts; one should always speak sweetly; to those who come to the house he should give bed, seat and food.
The guest whose hope is broken and who returns from a house takes away the merit of that person, giving him his own sin.
Disrespect, egoism, hypocrisy, slander, injury and harshness are not praised for a householder.
The householder who properly does this supreme rule is freed from all bonds and attains the best worlds.
When ripe in age, Brahmins, the householder who has done his duty should place his wife in his sons' care and go to the forest, or go with her.
Living on leaves, roots and fruits, bearing hair, beard and matted locks, sleeping on the ground, he should there be a sage, welcoming all guests.
He should make his lower and upper garments of hides, kasha and kusha; likewise bathing three times a day is recommended for him.
Worship of deities, fire-offering, honouring all who come, alms and offering of the bali are praised for him.
Anointing the limbs with forest oil is also praised; his austerity, best of Brahmins, is endurance of cold, heat and the like.
The forest-dweller, sage, who observes these fixed practices burns his faults like fire and conquers eternal worlds.
The fourth ashrama is declared by the wise to be that of the mendicant; as I tell its nature, understand, best ones.
He should abandon affection for sons, property and wife, best of Brahmins, and go to the fourth ashrama station, free of envy.
He should abandon all enterprises of the three varnas, best of Brahmins, being equal toward friends and the like and friendly to all creatures.
He should never harm by speech, mind or deed those born from womb or egg and so on, being disciplined, and should avoid all attachments.
One night's stay in a village, five nights' in a city; neither affection nor hatred arises in him toward animals.
For the maintenance of life he should wander to houses, begging, at a time when the cooking fire is out and people have eaten, of praised varnas.
In non-receipt he should not be dejected, nor rejoice in receipt; he should be only for the maintenance of life, freed from attachment to measure.
He should avoid honoured gains and condemnation from all sides; by honoured gains an ascetic, though liberated, is bound.
Having given up the faults of desire, anger, pride, greed, delusion and the like, the wanderer should be free of "mine."
One who roams the earth giving fearlessness to all beings, when released from the body, never has fear arise.
Having performed an Agnihotra established in his own body, the Brahmin offers into the bodily fire in his own mouth the oblations received as alms, and he goes to the worlds by that pyre-fire.
The twice-born who practises the ashrama of liberation as said, pure, with resolved intellect, goes to Brahma's world, tranquil like a fire without fuel.
Fallen from his own station he goes to mixing of varnas; a Brahmin, Kshatriya or Vaishya of such kind goes to Shudra-hood.
But a Shudra who by his own dharma is possessed of knowledge and wisdom, pure, knowing dharma and devoted to dharma, enjoys the fruit of dharma.
And this other thing, goddess, was told by Brahma: spiritual, final success is attained by those who serve dharma and desire.
Fierce food is despised, goddess; food of a group, shraddha and birth-impurity food, advertised food, or Shudra's food should never be eaten.
Shudra's food is always despised, goddess, by the great-souled gods; this, as declared from the Grandfather's mouth, is the authority, I think.
A twice-born who dies with the remainder of Shudra's food in his belly, a keeper of the fire and a sacrificer, would share the Shudra's state.
By that remainder of Shudra's food a Brahmin driven from Brahma's station goes to Shudra-hood; there is no deliberation there.
One who dies with the remainder of whose food in the belly, that womb that Brahmin goes to whose food he lives on.
One who, having obtained the rare happiness of being a Brahmin, disrespects it, or eats forbidden food, falls from twice-born-hood.
A drinker of liquor, killer of a Brahmin, thief, robber, one who has broken his vow, the impure, one without Vedic study, sinner, greedy, hostile, cheat,
one without vows, husband of a low-caste woman, eater from a pot, soma-seller, one serving the inferior: a Brahmin falls from Brahma's womb.
A violator of the teacher's bed, one who hates the teacher, one fond of reviling the teacher, or a hater of Brahmins falls from Brahma's womb.
By these good actions, goddess, practised, a Shudra may attain Brahmin-hood and a Vaishya may attain Kshatriya-hood.
A Shudra who does all actions justly by rule, serving all guests, eating from food-remnants,
who diligently does service and attendance to the eldest varna, undepressed, the best, constantly standing in the good path,
honouring gods and the twice-born, devoted to hospitality to all, approaching his wife at the proper season, restrained, eating moderately,
skilled, seeking good people, eating remnants of food, not eating meat in vain: the Shudra attains Vaishya-hood.
Truthful, free of ego-speech, free of dualities, knowing Sama, he sacrifices with constant sacrifices, devoted to Vedic study, pure,
self-controlled, honouring Brahmins, free of envy toward all varnas, observing the householder's vow, eating twice a day,
eating remnants, conquering his food, desireless, without egoism, attending to Agnihotra and offering by rule,
serving all guests, eating food of remnants, a Vaishya becomes twice-born with the three fires alone prescribed.
That Vaishya is born in a pure, great Kshatriya family; that Vaishya becomes a Kshatriya, refined from birth.
Initiated, intent on vows, he becomes twice-born, refined; he gives and sacrifices with abundant sacrifices with fees obtained.
Having studied, desiring heaven, always with the three fires as refuge, always giving with a wet hand, protecting subjects by dharma,
truthful, always doing true things, of pure sight, burnt by the rod of dharma, a fulfiller of dharma, desire and wealth,
controlled by the performance of duties, marked by the sixth part (tax), he should not serve rustic dharmas at will, skilled in wealth.
At the proper season the righteous-souled one should always approach his wife, always fasting, restrained, devoted to Vedic study, pure.
Always sleeping at home with an outer separation, doing hospitality to all, he is always glad-minded for the three aims.
Saying to Shudras desiring food, "It is always prepared," from his own interest or desire, he should look at nothing.
What he effects for the ancestors, gods and guests in his own house and attends by rule, and alms only,
offering Agnihotra twice a day by rule, killed in battle facing the foe for the benefit of cows and Brahmins,
entering purified by the mantras of the three fires he becomes twice-born, possessed of knowledge and wisdom, refined, a master of the Veda.
A Vaishya of righteous soul and a Kshatriya by his own action, goddess, from the fruits of these actions, born of lower birth or family,
even a Shudra endowed with the scriptures, refined, becomes twice-born; or a Brahmin of bad conduct who eats food of all kinds
abandoning Brahmin-hood becomes a Shudra of that kind. By pure actions, goddess, the pure-souled, sense-conquered
Shudra, too, should be served like the twice-born: so Brahma himself said. By nature and action, wherever a Shudra stands,
he should be known as purified by the twice-born, I think. Neither birth, nor sacrament, nor learning, nor lineage
are the causes of twice-born-hood; conduct alone is the cause. This whole Brahmin in the world is ordained by conduct.
A Shudra too, standing in conduct, goes to Brahmin-hood; the nature of Brahman, fair-hipped, is held by me as equal everywhere.
Where Brahman, free of qualities and stainless, stays, that one is twice-born. These pure ones, goddess, who show the station and state,
were themselves told by Brahma, the boon-giver, creating creatures. The great field of Brahma moves in the world like a foot (?).
What seed falls there — that is the cultivation that will bear fruit hereafter; one must always be content, always relying on the good path.
Having entered Brahma's path one wishing to prosper should live; the householder must be a reciter of the Samhita at home.
Always devoted to Vedic study, not living by study; the Brahmin who is thus, always standing in the good path,
keeping the fire, studying, is fit for becoming Brahman; having obtained Brahmin-hood, goddess, it must be guarded by the self-controlled.
By birth, acceptance and giving, and by actions, pure-smiling one — this secret has been told to you: how a Shudra may become twice-born, or a Brahmin fallen from dharma may attain Shudra-hood.
By what is a man bound by speech, or released again? Those actions, god, tell me, lord of beings, sinless one.

Those men who do not speak falsehood here for themselves or for others, or resting on unrighteousness, go to heaven.
brahmapuran:224:19	Those who for livelihood, for dharma, or by willfulness do not utter untruth go to heaven.
brahmapuran:224:20	Those who speak smooth speech, of clear sound, sweet and free of evil, with self-restraint, go to heaven.
brahmapuran:224:21	Those who do not speak harsh, bitter or cruel words, and not delighting in slander, being good, go to heaven.
brahmapuran:224:22	Those who do not speak slander, or what causes division of friends, or what causes pain to others, go to heaven.
brahmapuran:224:23	Men who avoid harshness and treachery to others, equal to all beings, self-controlled, go to heaven.
brahmapuran:224:24	Those refraining from deceitful prattle, avoiding the contrary, always speaking gently, go to heaven.
brahmapuran:224:25	Those who in anger do not utter speech that tears the heart, who find peace when angry, go to heaven.
brahmapuran:224:26	This dharma of speech, goddess, should always be served by men; falsehood should be avoided by the wise, with good qualities of truth.
By what action of mind is a man always bound? Tell me that, fortunate one, god of gods, bearer of the Pinaka.

Men joined here with dharma of the mind always go to heaven, auspicious one; hear that as I tell.
brahmapuran:224:29	By a badly directed mind, with inner form badly directed, a man is bound here; or hear that, fair-faced one:
brahmapuran:224:30	when another's property is seen left in a solitary forest, those who do not take it even in mind go to heaven.
brahmapuran:224:31	Likewise those who, acting out of desire, in private do not harm others' wives even in mind go to heaven.
brahmapuran:224:32	Men who always with equal mind treat enemy and friend with friendship, meeting, go to heaven.
brahmapuran:224:33	The learned, compassionate, pure, truthful, content with their own wealth go to heaven.
brahmapuran:224:34	Those without enmity, without strain, always fond of friendly thoughts, compassionate to all beings go to heaven.
brahmapuran:224:35	Those who know, who act, who are patient, dear to friends, always knowing dharma and adharma go to heaven.
brahmapuran:224:36	Those, goddess, who are without expectation about the accumulated fruit of good and bad actions go to heaven.
brahmapuran:224:37	Always devoted to gods and Brahmins, avoiding the sinful, having attained resolve, they go to heaven.
brahmapuran:224:38	These have been declared by me, goddess, with the fruits of good actions, devoted to the path of heaven; what more do you wish to hear?

I have a great doubt, Maheshvara, about mortals; therefore you ought to explain it carefully to me today.
brahmapuran:224:40	By what action does a man get long life, lord? Or by austerity, lord of gods, by what does one get great life?
brahmapuran:224:41	By what action on earth does a man become short-lived? You ought to tell, blameless one, the results of actions.
brahmapuran:224:42	Others are greatly fortunate, others ill-fortunate; some are of poor family, others of good family, and others are born so.
brahmapuran:224:43	Some men appear hard to look at, as if made of wood; others are pleasant to look at merely by sight.
brahmapuran:224:44	Some appear dull-witted, some appear learned, others greatly wise, possessing knowledge and wisdom.
brahmapuran:224:45	Some are of few words, others of great speech; men are seen thus, god; therefore you ought to explain.

Well, I shall tell you, goddess, the rising of the fruit of action, by which every man in the world of mortals experiences his own fruit.
brahmapuran:224:47	A man who kills living beings, bearing a rod in hand, a lord of yogis (cruel), always with raised weapon, kills hosts of beings.
brahmapuran:224:48	Merciless to all beings, constantly causing agitation, a refugeless one, very pitiless even to insects and moths —
brahmapuran:224:49	such a man, goddess, goes to hell; but the opposite, righteous-souled, is born in his own form.
brahmapuran:224:50	The violent-souled goes to hell; the non-violent goes to heaven; a man gets terrible, painful torment in hell.
